items.statement:
Assume countable choice. Let $B$ be a smooth closed three-ball and let $a\subset B$ be a smooth neat proper arc with endpoints $p,q$. Supply a boundary-parallelism disk: an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=a\cup\lambda$, where $\lambda\subset\partial B$ is an arc joining $p$ to $q$ and $\operatorname{int}D\subset\operatorname{int}B$. The disk is smooth with the compatible corner charts at the two endpoints. Let $U\subset\partial B$ be a smooth closed disk with $p\in\operatorname{int}U$ and $q\notin U$.

There is a diffeomorphism of triples from $(B,a,U)$ to the standard closed unit ball, its vertical diameter, and its lower closed hemisphere, taking $p$ to the lower pole and $q$ to the upper pole. More precisely, after any preliminary standardization of $(B,a)$ with these endpoint images, the correction standardizing the marked boundary window can be made by an ambient isotopy of that ball fixing its diameter pointwise. Thus specifying the boundary window adds no unidentified motion or twist of the proper arc.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.
A neat $k$-submanifold $S$ of an $n$-manifold with boundary has boundary charts simultaneously straightening $S$ and $\partial M$; in particular its induced boundary is $S\cap\partial M$.

derivations.claim: Extend the bridge disk a short distance across its interior boundary arc $a$, leaving its boundary on $\partial B$ along a slightly longer boundary arc near $\lambda$. This gives a disk $D'$ containing $a$ as a neat proper arc and meeting $\partial B$ in one boundary interval. The construction is local: extend the disk parametrization across $a$ in its smooth boundary charts, and at $p,q$ use the quadrant charts with $\partial B$ as one face; compactness permits a common narrow strip. The extension is embedded after shrinking, since its new strip is locally embedded and disjoint compact parts of the original disk remain separated. In the extended planar parameter domain, $a$ cuts $D'$ into the original bridge disk and a thin added disk strip. Their boundary parametrizations can be identified with those of two half-disks, matching the parametrization and collar of $a$, by [F2]. Glue these maps across the common collar. This identifies $D'$ with a standard disk and $a$ with a diameter. The finitely many corner charts at its endpoints are retained before rounding.

Take a small closed thickening $N$ of $D'$ in $B$. It is a rounded product $D'\times[-\delta,\delta]$ and meets $\partial B$ in one rectangle window $W$ around the boundary interval of $D'$. To obtain the product compatibly at $\partial B$, choose a transverse field to $D'$ tangent to $\partial B$ on that interval, using the half-slice charts of [F3]. The oriented normal direction of the disk chooses the same transverse cone in finitely many charts; a positive weighted sum stays transverse. Its short flow in [F4] is the required thickening. Compactness and local inverses give a common injective product neighborhood. The arc lies in $D'\times\{0\}$ with endpoints in the interior of $W$ and otherwise in the interior of $N$. Under the disk coordinates of step 1.1 this is the diameter in the central disk of a rounded cylinder. Round the cylinder convexly away from those endpoints and rescale its normal coordinate. A radial diffeomorphism to a round ball preserves that central diameter: choose its radial scaling constant near the origin and interpolate to the positive boundary-radius function over a long logarithmic radial interval, so the radial derivative stays positive. Hence $(N,a)$ is a standard ball with diameter.

The complement $K=\overline{B\setminus N}$ is a ball by the reverse ball-window removal assertion of [F1], since $N$ is a ball meeting $\partial B$ in the one disk $W$. Moreover $B=N\cup K$ is their boundary sum along the other boundary disk of $N$. This attaching disk and the whole $K$ miss $a$, whose endpoints lie in the interior of $W$. Absorb $K$ into $N$ by [F1], choosing its attaching collar disjoint from $a$. The resulting diffeomorphism $(B,a)\to(N,a)$ fixes the arc. Combine it with the standardization of step 2.1, choosing the order of the two diameter endpoints so that $p$ goes to the lower pole and $q$ to the upper pole. This proves the unmarked assertion using the actual bridge disk.

Work now in that standard ball. On its boundary sphere the image of $U$ contains the lower pole and misses the upper pole. The shrinking and linearization proof in [F1], applied in dimension two with the disk center at the lower pole, gives an isotopy carrying $U$ to a sufficiently small round latitude disk about that pole, fixing the pole throughout. In detail the shrinking disk embeddings $e(r(t)x)$ fix $e(0)=p$; their linear interpolation also fixes $p$; their velocities therefore vanish there. Choose every extension neighborhood disjoint from $q$, since the whole shrinking track lies in $U$. Use a standard sphere chart at $p$ for the final linearization. Enlarge the resulting latitude disk to the lower hemisphere by latitude disks, still fixing both poles. The associated boundary isotopy $h_t$ thus fixes $p,q$ pointwise, though it can rotate their surrounding directions.

Extend this sphere isotopy over the ball fixing the diameter pointwise. Its boundary velocity vanishes at both endpoints. In endpoint coordinates $(x,y,z)$ where the sphere is $z=0$ and the diameter is the positive $z$-axis, extend that tangential velocity independently of $z$ and multiply by a cutoff. It then vanishes along the diameter axis. Away from the endpoint charts choose a thin boundary collar missing the remaining compact diameter subarc, extend there with a cutoff, and use a finite partition to join the extensions. All terms have the prescribed boundary value, are tangent to the boundary, and vanish on the diameter. Such a finite partition is obtained by finitely many coordinate bumps divided by their positive sum near the compact boundary track, then cut off in a common boundary neighborhood. The field has compact support, so [F4] supplies its ball-preserving flow, fixing the diameter and extending $h_t$ by uniqueness. This proves that any rotation near an endpoint in step 4.1 adds no motion of the arc itself.

The composite of the preliminary pair diffeomorphism of step 3.1 and the diameter-fixed correction of step 5.1 is a diffeomorphism of the required triples. The same correction applies after any preliminary endpoint-ordered standardization, because its only input is the marked sphere disk containing the lower pole and missing the upper one. This proves both assertions.

items.statement:
Assume countable choice. Let $L$ be a smooth link and $S$ a smooth closed embedded surface in $S^3$. Supply a smooth closed ball $W$ and a disk $U\subset\partial W$ such that $W\cap S=U$, and put $V=\overline{\partial W\setminus U}$. Suppose $L\cap W$ is a neat proper boundary-parallel arc $a$ with endpoints $p\in\operatorname{int}U$ and $q\in\operatorname{int}V$, with an actual boundary-parallelism disk supplied. Thus $U$ contains precisely one transverse link intersection.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be closed with $K\cap V=\varnothing$. Then an ambient isotopy preserving $L$ setwise, supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $W$, takes $S$ to a surface that agrees with $S$ outside $\operatorname{int}U$ and replaces $U$ by a disk disjoint from $K$. It fixes a collar of $\partial U$ in $S$, and the new puncture lies arbitrarily close to $q$ on $a$. In particular the old intersections $U\cap K$ are deleted without affecting other surface pieces. Link preservation here is setwise: its intersection point with the moving window travels along $a$.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] to identify $W$ with the unit ball in coordinates $(x,y,z)$, with $a$ the vertical diameter, $U$ the lower hemisphere and $V$ the upper hemisphere. Write $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $f(r)=-\sqrt{1-r^2}$ for the lower graph on $r<1$. Because $K$ is closed and misses the compact upper hemisphere, a sufficiently small neighborhood of that whole hemisphere in $W$ misses $K$. Likewise a sufficiently small neighborhood of its equatorial boundary circle in $W$ misses $K$. The surface outside $U$ misses the ball interior and meets its boundary only along $\partial U$, by hypothesis.

Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\theta$ that is one for $r\le1-2\delta$ and zero for $r\ge1-\delta$, with $\delta>0$ small. For a small $\epsilon>0$ define $g(r)=\theta(r)(2-\epsilon)\sqrt{1-r^2}$. This is smooth as a function of $(x,y)$ on the whole plane after extension by zero, since its support is inside $r<1$. The graph $z=f(r)+g(r)$ agrees with $U$ near the equator. On $r\le1-2\delta$ it is $(1-\epsilon)\sqrt{1-r^2}$, arbitrarily close to the upper hemisphere; on the remaining annulus it stays inside the ball and has distance tending uniformly to zero from the equatorial circle as $\delta\to0$. Choose $\delta$ first for the equatorial neighborhood of step 1.1, then $\epsilon$ for the upper-hemisphere neighborhood. The resulting disk misses $K$. Its axis point is $z=1-\epsilon$, so can be arbitrarily close to $q$.

Move through the graphs $z=f(r)+t g(r)$, $0\le t\le1$, retaining the unchanged hemisphere collar where $g=0$. These form a smooth isotopy of disks, since every moving point is in the compact region $r\le1-\delta$, where graph coordinates are smooth, and the complement is stationary. All disks meet the vertical axis transversely exactly once, at $z=-1+t(2-\epsilon)$. On a small neighborhood of the compact moving track use the vertical field $X_t=g(r)\psi(z-f(r)-t g(r))\partial_z$, where $\psi=1$ near zero and is supported in a small normal interval. Multiply by a further spatial cutoff equal to one on the moving track and zero outside its chosen neighborhood. The field has the prescribed graph velocity. It is vertical along the axis, so preserves the axis setwise; it is zero near the equator. The initial track meets the boundary of $W$ only in the interior of $U$, and the later nonstationary track is in $\operatorname{int}W$. Thus the field can be supported away from every stationary surface piece.

Transfer this field back to a neighborhood of its track in $S^3$. In the interior of $W$ the ball diffeomorphism supplies the coordinates directly. Across the initial face $U$, its coordinate functions extend smoothly to boundary charts, and their full-rank differential gives an extension to a common narrow neighborhood. At $p$, take the extension in the simultaneous arc-boundary chart of [F3], retaining the vertical axis as $L$ on both sides; it agrees with the already prescribed coordinates along the inside axis. One constructs this relative extension by extending its coordinate functions off the half-space and then subtracting their unwanted transverse values on the exterior axis, using an axis cutoff: those values and all their jets vanish at the boundary point because the interior axis was already straight. Hence the correction is smooth across the boundary and does not alter the inside chart; a small extension keeps the differential invertible. Compactness and the local inverse property give a common injective neighborhood for the compact initial moving patch. Other portions of $L$ and of $S\setminus\operatorname{int}U$ are disjoint from the moving track, so shrinking the neighborhood avoids them. The transferred field is therefore tangent to the actual link wherever its support meets it, is zero on all other link components, and can be extended by zero within the prescribed neighborhood of $W$.

Apply [F2] to this compactly supported field. Uniqueness makes its flow carry the old disk to the prescribed graphs, while every stationary surface piece remains fixed. The field's restriction to $L$ is tangent, so both forward and reverse uniqueness preserve $L$ setwise. At time one the new disk misses $K$ by step 2.1 and its unique puncture is the point near $q$ specified there. The collar of $\partial U$ and the rest of $S$ were outside the support. This proves all support, fixed-piece and puncture-motion claims.
